title: The Suez Canal: why it is strategic
subtitle: 1869 to present
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: A 193 kilometer water corridor carries 12% of global trade. A single stranded ship in 2021 was enough to paralyze the planet: welcome to **Suez**.

hero.hook: 193 kilometers of canal, 12% of world trade: this is the story of the most strategic passage in the world.

blocks.text: The **Suez** Canal in Egypt is one of the most strategic crossing points on the planet. By connecting the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea, it saves ships from having to circumnavigate the whole of Africa via the **Cloak of Good Hope**, shortening the journey between Europe and Asia by almost 7,000 kilometers.

Beyond its economic role, this channel is a true barometer of global power relations. From its colonial construction to its nationalization by Egypt in 1956, to today's maritime tensions, it remains a major sovereignty issue.

sections.title: The Colonial Era: A Bridge to Empire

blocks.text: The drilling of the Isthmus of Suez was led by the French engineer Ferdinand de Lesseps. Between 1859 and 1869, thousands of Egyptian workers dug this 193 kilometer waterway.

blocks.caption: The inauguration of the Suez Canal in November 1869 marked the culmination of a decade of titanic work.

blocks.text: When it was inaugurated in 1869, the canal was managed by a private company with mainly French capital. Great Britain, initially skeptical, quickly understood the importance of this route for its colonies. Taking advantage of the enormous debts of the khedive, the sovereign of Egypt, she bought her shares in 1875 and became the main shareholder.
During the inauguration in 1869, the composer Giuseppe Verdi was commissioned to write an opera for the occasion: this is how the famous work “Aida” was born.

This foreign domination creates growing tensions. For most of the 20th century, the canal was seen by Egyptian nationalists as a symbol of colonial humiliation, a British enclave at the heart of a country seeking independence.

The year 1956 marked a historic break. Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser, a **[[Pan-Arabism]]** figure, nationalized the canal company on July 26, 1956. His objective was to finance, with revenues from the canal, a large dam on the Nile from which the Western powers had just withdrawn their financing.

The reaction was immediate: France and the United Kingdom, who were losing their interests, joined forces with Israel to launch a secret military offensive. The canal was occupied, but the operation angered American President Eisenhower, who had not been informed and feared that this aggression would push the Third World towards the side of the USSR.

Under American pressure, the European powers are forced into a humiliating withdrawal. It was the end of the leading role of France and the United Kingdom as colonial powers, and the triumph of Nasser, who had become an idol in the Arab world. This episode remains known as . **[[The Suez Crisis (1956)]]**

sections.title: A vital artery in the face of modern crises

blocks.text: Today, the Suez Canal remains the heart of global maritime trade: around 12% of world trade and nearly 20,000 ships pass through it each year. But its narrowness, faced with the gigantism of modern ships, constitutes a major vulnerability.

On March 26, 2021, the giant container ship  ran aground across the canal, blocking all traffic for six days. The obstruction is causing a traffic jam of more than 400 ships and costing the global economy an estimated $400 million per hour. **[[Ever Given (March 2021)]]**

blocks.caption: In March 2021, the container ship Ever Given blocked the Suez Canal for six days.

blocks.text: Beyond the technical aspect, regional geopolitics also threatens this stability. Between 2023 and 2024, missile attacks carried out by the **[[Houthis]]** from Yemen against commercial ships forced many shipowners to divert their fleets through southern Africa, a three-week detour that greatly increases costs.

To remain competitive, Egypt launched the “new Suez Canal” in 2015, which doubles passage capacities on certain sections. The canal is also becoming an economic zone attracting Chinese and European investments.

Canal revenues remain one of the main sources of foreign exchange for Egypt, making the country extremely vigilant about the security of the **Bab-el-Mandeb** Strait, the true southern gateway to the entire Suez system.

The Suez Canal, inaugurated in 1869, went from a tool of British imperial domination to a symbol of Egyptian sovereignty after the crisis of 1956. Today, it carries 12% of world trade, but remains vulnerable to technical incidents and tensions in the Red Sea.
